title: Joins
summary_md: Combine tables correctly: inner vs outer joins, FULL OUTER in MySQL, cross and self-joins, semi/anti-joins, the ON vs WHERE trap on LEFT JOINs, and fan-out from joining two child tables.

sections.heading: INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN
sections.body_md:
- `INNER JOIN` keeps only rows with a match on both sides. `JOIN` alone means INNER.
- `LEFT JOIN` keeps **every left row**; right-side columns are NULL where nothing matched.
- Join condition in `ON`; use table aliases and qualify columns (`o.customer_id`).
- To count related rows including zero, `LEFT JOIN` then `COUNT(right.key)`.
- `USING (col)` is shorthand for equal-named columns in MySQL; SQL Server has no USING - write the ON.
- Join on keys that are unique on at least one side, or you multiply rows (see fan-out).

syntax.mysql: FROM a [INNER | LEFT [OUTER]] JOIN b ON a.key = b.key
syntax.tsql: FROM a [INNER | LEFT [OUTER]] JOIN b ON a.key = b.key

args.name: a
args.meaning: Left table: its rows are all kept in a LEFT JOIN.

args.name: b
args.meaning: Right table: contributes NULLs when no match.

args.name: ON a.key = b.key
args.meaning: Match condition evaluated per pair of rows; may include extra predicates.

examples.title: INNER JOIN drops customers without orders
examples.explain_md: Customer 6 (no orders) is missing: only customers with at least one order appear.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: LEFT JOIN keeps them, with a 0
examples.explain_md: Same query, LEFT JOIN, COUNT on a right-table column: customer 6 appears with 0 orders.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: What the unmatched row looks like
examples.explain_md: The padded columns are NULL. This is why `WHERE o.order_id IS NULL` finds unmatched left rows.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IN (5, 6)
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IN (5, 6)
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;

pitfalls_md: `COUNT(*)` after a LEFT JOIN counts the NULL-padded row as 1. Count a right-table column.

sections.heading: RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN
sections.body_md:
- `RIGHT JOIN` = `LEFT JOIN` with the tables swapped. Most people only write LEFT; swap the order instead.
- `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from **both** sides. SQL Server supports it; **MySQL does not**.
- MySQL emulation: `LEFT JOIN` UNION ALL the right-only rows (`RIGHT JOIN ... WHERE left.key IS NULL`). Use UNION ALL plus the anti filter; plain UNION would also dedupe legitimate duplicate rows.
- Typical use: reconcile two sources and see what is missing from each side.

examples.title: RIGHT JOIN equals swapped LEFT JOIN
examples.explain_md: orders RIGHT JOIN customers returns exactly the rows of customers LEFT JOIN orders.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM orders AS o
RIGHT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM orders AS o
RIGHT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: FULL OUTER JOIN and the MySQL emulation
examples.explain_md: Five rows: matched pairs, Cy with no badge, and the orphan badge with no student. MySQL needs LEFT JOIN + right-only rows.

tables.name: students
tables.description_md: One row per student. Cy has no badges.

tables.name: badges
tables.description_md: One row per badge. Badge 13 points at student 9, who does not exist (orphan).

examples.mysql:
SELECT student_id, name, badge_id, badge
FROM (
  SELECT s.student_id, s.name, b.badge_id, b.badge, b.student_id AS badge_owner
  FROM students AS s
  LEFT JOIN badges AS b ON b.student_id = s.student_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.student_id, s.name, b.badge_id, b.badge, b.student_id
  FROM students AS s
  RIGHT JOIN badges AS b ON b.student_id = s.student_id
  WHERE s.student_id IS NULL
) AS f
ORDER BY COALESCE(student_id, badge_owner), badge_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT s.student_id, s.name, b.badge_id, b.badge
FROM students AS s
FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.student_id = s.student_id
ORDER BY COALESCE(s.student_id, b.student_id), b.badge_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; the first form emulates it. SQL Server uses FULL OUTER JOIN directly.

pitfalls_md: Using `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` in the emulation silently removes duplicate rows.

sections.heading: CROSS JOIN and self-joins
sections.body_md:
- `CROSS JOIN` = every left row with every right row (n x m). No ON clause. Use it to build grids (dates x regions) then LEFT JOIN facts onto the grid to expose gaps.
- A **self-join** joins a table to itself under two aliases: hierarchy (employee -> manager) or pairs (two rows of the same group).
- Hierarchy: use `LEFT JOIN` so the top of the tree (no manager) is kept.
- Pairs: add `a.id < b.id` to avoid (x, x) and mirrored duplicates.

examples.title: Find missing days with a calendar grid
examples.explain_md: Every (region, date) pair is built with CROSS JOIN, then the real rows are LEFT JOINed. NULL revenue marks the days West had no sales.
examples.mysql:
SELECT r.region, d.sale_date
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT region FROM daily_sales) AS r
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT sale_date FROM daily_sales) AS d
LEFT JOIN daily_sales AS s
       ON s.region = r.region AND s.sale_date = d.sale_date
WHERE s.revenue IS NULL
ORDER BY r.region, d.sale_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT r.region, d.sale_date
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT region FROM daily_sales) AS r
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT sale_date FROM daily_sales) AS d
LEFT JOIN daily_sales AS s
       ON s.region = r.region AND s.sale_date = d.sale_date
WHERE s.revenue IS NULL
ORDER BY r.region, d.sale_date;

examples.title: Employee and manager name
examples.explain_md: Same table twice: `e` is the employee, `m` the manager. Ana (the CEO) has no manager; LEFT JOIN keeps her with NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

examples.title: Pairs inside a group
examples.explain_md: `a.emp_id < b.emp_id` yields each Sales pair once and never pairs someone with themselves.
examples.mysql:
SELECT a.name AS emp_a, b.name AS emp_b
FROM employees AS a
JOIN employees AS b ON a.dept = b.dept AND a.emp_id < b.emp_id
WHERE a.dept = 'Sales'
ORDER BY a.emp_id, b.emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT a.name AS emp_a, b.name AS emp_b
FROM employees AS a
JOIN employees AS b ON a.dept = b.dept AND a.emp_id < b.emp_id
WHERE a.dept = 'Sales'
ORDER BY a.emp_id, b.emp_id;

sections.heading: Semi-join and anti-join
sections.body_md:
- **Semi-join** = rows from A that *have* a match in B, with no columns from B and **no duplicates**: `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.k = A.k)`.
- **Anti-join** = rows from A with *no* match: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)`, or `LEFT JOIN B ... WHERE B.k IS NULL`.
- A plain JOIN as a filter duplicates A rows when B has many matches; EXISTS does not.
- `NOT IN (subquery)` breaks if the subquery returns a NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS.
- All three anti-join forms give the same rows; NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN/IS NULL are the safe ones.

examples.title: Customers with at least one completed order
examples.explain_md: One row per qualifying customer even though customer 1 has three completed orders.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: Customers with no completed order
examples.explain_md: Pablo (4) only has a refunded order and pablo diaz (6) has none.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: Same result with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
examples.explain_md: The status filter must live in ON, not WHERE, otherwise the unmatched rows are filtered out before the IS NULL test.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

pitfalls_md: `SELECT 1` inside EXISTS is convention only; the select list is ignored.

sections.heading: Filter in ON vs WHERE (LEFT JOIN)
sections.body_md:
- For **INNER** joins, ON and WHERE filters are equivalent.
- For **LEFT** joins they differ:
  - A condition on the right table in `ON` only limits which right rows can match; every left row survives (padded with NULLs).
  - The same condition in `WHERE` runs after the join and removes the NULL-padded rows, silently turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
- Put left-table filters in WHERE; put right-table filters in ON when you want to keep unmatched left rows.

examples.title: Right-table filter in ON keeps all customers
examples.explain_md: All six customers appear; customer 6 gets 0.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS completed_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS completed_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: Same filter in WHERE loses customers
examples.explain_md: Customer 6 vanishes: the NULL status fails `status = 'completed'`. The query is now an inner join in disguise.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS completed_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS completed_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

sections.heading: Fan-out: double counting across two child tables
sections.body_md:
- Joining a parent to **two** one-to-many children produces `children_1 x children_2` rows per parent. Sums on either child are inflated.
- Symptoms: totals larger than the source table's total; counts that look like products.
- Fix: **aggregate each child to the parent's grain first** (derived table / CTE), then join the one-row-per-parent results.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT id)` can rescue counts but never sums (equal amounts collapse); do not rely on it.
- Always sanity-check: `SUM` after the join vs `SUM` on the base table.

examples.title: Wrong: join both children, then SUM
examples.explain_md: Acme has 2 invoices x 3 payments = 6 rows, so invoiced shows 900 (true 300) and paid shows 120 (true 60).

tables.name: invoices
tables.description_md: Acme has two invoices (100 + 200); Birch has one (50).

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: Acme has three payments (10 + 20 + 30); Birch has one (50).

examples.mysql:
SELECT a.name,
       SUM(i.amount) AS invoiced,
       SUM(p.amount) AS paid
FROM accounts AS a
JOIN invoices AS i ON i.account_id = a.account_id
JOIN payments AS p ON p.account_id = a.account_id
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.name
ORDER BY a.account_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT a.name,
       SUM(i.amount) AS invoiced,
       SUM(p.amount) AS paid
FROM accounts AS a
JOIN invoices AS i ON i.account_id = a.account_id
JOIN payments AS p ON p.account_id = a.account_id
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.name
ORDER BY a.account_id;

examples.title: Right: pre-aggregate each child
examples.explain_md: Each child is reduced to one row per account before joining, so no multiplication occurs. Use LEFT JOINs (plus COALESCE) if an account may lack invoices or payments.

tables.name: invoices
tables.description_md: Acme has two invoices (100 + 200); Birch has one (50).

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: Acme has three payments (10 + 20 + 30); Birch has one (50).

examples.mysql:
SELECT a.name,
       COALESCE(i.invoiced, 0) AS invoiced,
       COALESCE(p.paid, 0)     AS paid
FROM accounts AS a
LEFT JOIN (SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS invoiced
           FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id) AS i ON i.account_id = a.account_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS paid
           FROM payments GROUP BY account_id) AS p ON p.account_id = a.account_id
ORDER BY a.account_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT a.name,
       COALESCE(i.invoiced, 0) AS invoiced,
       COALESCE(p.paid, 0)     AS paid
FROM accounts AS a
LEFT JOIN (SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS invoiced
           FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id) AS i ON i.account_id = a.account_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS paid
           FROM payments GROUP BY account_id) AS p ON p.account_id = a.account_id
ORDER BY a.account_id;

pitfalls_md: A fan-out never raises an error; the numbers are just wrong. Compare against an independent total.
